questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Take the second away from the first and display [difference] and nothing else.

teach.say: - subtracts and + adds. They work on numbers, so cast each input with int() first.

brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
The difference may be negative.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one difference out

tests.why: A crash or a joined-up answer means the inputs were still text. Cast each one with int() before subtracting.
Two equal numbers give 0, which is a real answer. An empty line means nothing was printed.
5 instead of -5 means you subtracted the other way round. Keep the order the question gives, even below zero.

questions.fb: Arithmetic works on numbers only, so anything that came from input() is cast with int() before you touch it.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Multiply them together and display [product] and nothing else.

teach.say: * multiplies two numbers. If one side is still text, * repeats the text instead, so cast both with int().

brief: The user types in two whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one product out

tests.why: A long row of repeated digits means a string was multiplied: '6' * 7 repeats the text. Cast both with int().
Anything multiplied by 0 is 0, which is a real answer and still has to be printed.
Printing one of the numbers back means the multiplication is missing.

questions.fb: * on two numbers multiplies, but * on a string repeats it, so the cast decides which of the two you get.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Divide the first by the second and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: In Python / always gives a real number, so the answer keeps a decimal part even when it divides exactly.

brief: The second number is never 0.
Use / , so the answer is a real number.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one division out

tests.why: 4 instead of 4.5 means // was used, which throws the fraction away.
4 instead of 4.0 means the answer was cast back to an integer. / keeps the decimal part even when it divides exactly.
2 instead of 1.75 means the answer was rounded. Print the division as it comes out.

questions.fb: In Python / always gives a real number, which matters when you print it: 4.0 and 4 are not the same output.

questions.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Add all three together and display [total] and nothing else.

teach.say: A calculation can use as many values as you like, as long as every one of them has been cast to a number.

brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
questions.starter: # Three whole numbers in, one total out

tests.why: 566 instead of 17 means the three lines were joined as text. Cast every one with int().
Missing one of the numbers out gives a smaller total. All three lines have to be read.
Three inputs need three separate input() calls, one for each line.

questions.fb: Every value in a calculation has to be a number first, however many of them there are.

questions.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Add the first two together, multiply that answer by the third, and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: Python does * and / before + and - , so brackets are how you force an addition to happen first.

brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
Brackets decide the order, because * is worked out before + .
questions.starter: # Three whole numbers in. Add two, then multiply.

tests.why: 14 means the brackets are missing, so Python multiplied 3 by 4 before adding the 2.
13 means only the first two were added. The third number multiplies the whole of that answer.
A 0 is still a number to be read, and adding it changes nothing, which is the right answer here.

questions.fb: Operators have an order, and brackets are how you say the order you actually want.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Work out how many whole times the second goes into the first and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: // divides and throws the fraction away, so it says how many whole lots fit. OCR calls it DIV.

brief: The second number is never 0.
Use // , which leaves a whole number.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, whole lots out

tests.why: 7.8333 means / was used. A part lot is not a whole one, so use // , which leaves a whole number.
4.0 instead of 4 means / was used and it divided exactly. // gives a whole number with no decimal part.
1 instead of 0 means you rounded up. Six goes into five no whole times at all.

questions.fb: // is division that keeps only the whole lots, and it rounds down rather than to the nearest.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Work out what is left over when the first is divided by the second and display [remainder] and nothing else.

teach.say: % gives what is left over after a whole division. OCR calls it MOD.

brief: The second number is never 0.
Use % , which gives the remainder.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, the remainder out

tests.why: 7 means // was used, which gives the whole lots rather than what is left behind.
An exact division leaves 0, and that 0 still has to be printed.
When the first number is the smaller one, none of it is used up, so all of it is left over.

questions.fb: % is the partner of // : one takes the whole lots away, the other reports what they left behind.

questions.q: Ask the user for one whole number. Divide it by the fixed number 8. Display [whole lots], then [what is left over] on the next line.

teach.say: The number you divide by can be a fixed one. // gives the whole lots and % the remainder, so between them nothing is lost.

brief: The 8 is fixed in your program, not typed in.
Use // for the first line and % for the second.
questions.starter: # One whole number in. Whole lots, then the remainder.

tests.why: 6.25 means / was used on the first line. // leaves a whole number.
This one divides exactly, so nothing is left. An empty second line means the % is missing.
Fewer than 8 means 0 whole lots and all 5 left over. A 1 here means the division rounded up.

questions.fb: // and % answer two halves of the same question, and a fixed divisor works exactly like one that was typed in.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Display [how many whole times the second goes into the first], then [what is left over] on the next line.

teach.say: // and % are a pair: // says how many whole lots fit, % says what is left behind. Together they lose nothing.

brief: The second number is never 0.
Use // for the first line and % for the second.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in. Whole lots, then the remainder.

tests.why: 7.6 means / was used. The first line is whole lots only, so it needs // .
They divide exactly here, so the second line is 0. An empty line means the % is missing.
0 whole lots and 3 left over. A 1 on the first line means the division rounded up.

questions.fb: Multiply the whole lots by the divisor, add the remainder, and you are back where you started: that is what makes them a pair.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Raise it to the power 2 and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 5 is 2 multiplied by itself five times.

brief: The user types in one whole number.
Use ** , not ^ , which means something else in Python.
questions.starter: # One whole number in, the power 2 out

tests.why: 8 instead of 16 means you multiplied by 2. The power 2 means 4 times 4, written 4 ** 2.
14 means you multiplied by 2 again. A number to the power 2 is that number times itself.
1 to the power 2 is still 1, which looks suspicious but is right.

questions.fb: ** is the power operator, and watch out for ^ , which looks like a power in maths but does something else in Python.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Raise it to the power 3 and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: The power says how many times the number is multiplied by itself, so ** 3 is three of them multiplied together.

brief: The user types in one whole number.
Use ** , not ^ .
questions.starter: # One whole number in, the power 3 out

tests.why: 12 means you multiplied by 3. The power 3 means 4 times 4 times 4, written 4 ** 3.
49 means the power 2 was used. Check the number after the ** .
A power of 10 is easy to check by counting the zeros: three of them for the power 3.

questions.fb: Changing the number after ** changes how many times the value is multiplied by itself, and nothing else.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Raise the fixed number 2 to that power and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: Either side of ** can be a variable. Here the number being raised is fixed and the power is the one that varies.

brief: The 2 is fixed in your program; the power is what the user types in.
Use ** , not ^ .
questions.starter: # One whole number in, 2 to that power out

tests.why: 25 means the two values are the wrong way round. The 2 goes before the ** and the input after it.
20 means you multiplied instead of raising to a power.
Anything to the power 0 is 1. A 0 here means the input was used as the number being raised.

questions.fb: The order matters: a ** b and b ** a are different sums, so read which value is the power.

questions.q: Ask the user for a number, which may have a decimal point. Work out its square root and display [answer] and nothing else.

teach.say: The power 0.5 is the square root, and it always gives a real number.

brief: The user types in one number, which may have a decimal point.
Cast it with float(), not int().
Raise it to the power 0.5.
questions.starter: # One number in, its square root out

tests.why: 40.5 means the number was halved rather than rooted. The power 0.5 undoes the power 2.
A crash here means int() was used, and int() cannot handle a decimal point. Use float().
10 instead of 10.0 means the answer was cast back to an integer. A fractional power always gives a real number.

questions.fb: Raising to the power 0.5 is the square root, and the answer is a real number even for a perfect square.

questions.q: Ask the user for a number, which may have a decimal point. Use round() to display [the number to the nearest whole number] and nothing else.

teach.say: round(x) rounds to the nearest whole number. int(x) is a different thing: it throws the decimals away without looking at them.

brief: The user types in one number, which may have a decimal point.
Cast it with float(), then round it.
questions.starter: # One number in, the nearest whole number out

tests.why: 4 means int() was used, which cuts the decimals off instead of looking at them.
3 means you rounded up regardless. round() goes to whichever whole number is nearer.
9 means the decimals were thrown away. 9.8 is nearer to 10 than to 9.

questions.fb: round() looks at the decimals and goes to the nearer whole number, while int() simply drops them.

questions.q: Ask the user for a number, which may have a decimal point. Use round() to display [the number to 2 decimal places] and nothing else.

teach.say: A second number inside round() says how many decimal places to keep.

brief: The user types in one number, which may have a decimal point.
Cast it with float(), then round it to 2 decimal places.
questions.starter: # One number in, 2 decimal places out

tests.why: 5 means the second number inside round() is missing, so it rounded to a whole number.
2.35 means you rounded up. The third decimal is a 1, so the second one stays as it is.
Rounding 9.999 to 2 places carries all the way to 10.0, and Python drops the trailing zero.

questions.fb: round() takes a second number for the decimal places to keep, which is how a long answer is made readable.

questions.q: Ask the user for two whole numbers. Divide the first by the second and display [the answer to 1 decimal place] and nothing else.

teach.say: Dividing often leaves a long string of decimals. round(x, 1) keeps one decimal place and tidies the rest away.

brief: The second number is never 0.
Divide with / , then round the answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.starter: # Two whole numbers in, one rounded answer out

tests.why: 3.3333333333333335 means the division is right but the round() is missing.
4 means // was used. Divide with / first, then round what comes out.
4 instead of 4.0: / gives a real number and round() leaves it real, so the decimal part still shows.

questions.fb: Rounding is something you do to an answer, so the division happens first and round() tidies the result.

questions.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Work out their average, rounded to 1 decimal place, and display [average] and nothing else.

teach.say: Add the values inside brackets so the whole total is divided, then round what comes out.

brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
Add all three before dividing: brackets decide the order.
questions.starter: # Three whole numbers in, one rounded average out

tests.why: 5.666666666666667 means the division is right but the round() is missing. 5 means // was used instead of / .
This average is exact, and / still gives a real number, so the answer is 8.0 and not 8.
Add all three before dividing: (a + b + c) / 3. Without the brackets only the last one is divided.

questions.fb: An average is a total divided by how many there were, and the brackets are what make the whole total get divided.

questions.q: Ask the user for a seed to start the random number generator. Display [one random whole number from 1 to 6] and nothing else.

teach.say: random.randint(1, 6) picks a whole number from 1 to 6, and both ends can come up. Seeding first fixes the numbers, so the same seed always gives the same ones.

brief: Start with import random, then random.seed(int(input())). The user types in one whole number, the seed.
Use randint(1, 6), which can give 1 and 6 as well as everything between.
questions.starter: # Import random, seed it from the input, then one number

tests.why: A different number usually means the wrong ends: randrange(1, 6) stops at 5, and randint(1, 7) can give a 7.
The same answer for every seed means the seed was never used. Seed the generator with the number typed in.
Seeding after the number is drawn is too late. The seed has to be set first.

questions.fb: A seeded random sequence is fixed, which is the only way random code can be marked at all.

questions.q: Ask the user for a seed to start the random number generator. Display [first number], then [second number] on the next line, each a random whole number from 1 to 6.

teach.say: Each call to randint gives a new number. It never hands the same one back, so two numbers need two calls.

brief: Start with import random, then random.seed(int(input())). The user types in one whole number, the seed.
Use randint(1, 6) for both numbers.
questions.starter: # Import random, seed it from the input, then two numbers

tests.why: Different numbers from these usually means the wrong ends: randrange(1, 6) stops at 5, and randint(1, 7) can give a 7.
Two identical numbers mean one was stored and printed twice. Two numbers needs two separate calls.
If the first line matches but the second does not, the random module was called an extra time. Every call moves the sequence on.

questions.fb: Every call to randint moves the sequence on by one, so calling it twice is what gives you two different numbers.

questions.q: Ask the user for a seed to start the random number generator. Display three random whole numbers from 10 to 20, one on each line, then [total] on the next line.

teach.say: Store each random number in a variable as you make it, then add the variables. Calling randint again gives a new number, never the same one back.

brief: Start with import random, then random.seed(int(input())). The user types in one whole number, the seed.
Use randint(10, 20) for all three numbers.
Four lines of output: the three numbers, then their total.
questions.starter: # Import random, seed it from the input, then three numbers and a total

tests.why: If the three numbers are right but the total is not, randint was called again inside the total. That draws a fourth number.
Both ends turn up in these tests. A missing 20 points at randrange(10, 20), which stops at 19; a missing 10 points at randint(11, 20).
A different order from these means something called the random module before your three draws.

questions.fb: Use a variable for every random number you need more than once, because randint never hands the same one back.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number of pence. Display [whole pounds in that amount], then [pence left over] on the next line.

teach.say: There are 100 pence in a pound, so // 100 gives the whole pounds and % 100 gives the pence that are left.

brief: There are 100 pence in a pound, and the 100 is fixed in your program, not typed in.
Use // for the pounds and % for the pence.
questions.starter: # Pence in. Whole pounds, then the pence left over.

tests.why: 3.96 means / was used. The pounds line is whole pounds only, so it needs // .
Exactly one pound leaves 0 pence over, and that 0 still has to be printed.
Less than a pound gives 0 pounds and all 45 pence left over.

questions.fb: Breaking a quantity into bigger units and a remainder is always the same pair: // for the units, % for what is left.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Display [the number to the power 2], then [its square root to 2 decimal places] on the next line.

teach.say: Two calculations on the same value: store it once, then use that variable in both of them.

brief: The user types in one whole number.
Use ** for both: the power 2 and the power 0.5.
Round the square root to 2 decimal places.
questions.starter: # One whole number in. Power 2, then the rounded root.

tests.why: 3.1622776601683795 means the round() is missing from the second line.
2 instead of 2.0 means the root was cast to an integer. Rounding a real number leaves it real.
1.0 means int() was used somewhere, and 1.42 means you rounded up: the third decimal is a 4, so the second stays.

questions.fb: A rounded answer is still a real number, so a whole-looking root like 2.0 keeps its decimal part.

questions.q: Ask the user for three whole numbers. Display [total], then [their average to 1 decimal place] on the next line.

teach.say: Work the total out once and store it, then use that variable again instead of adding everything up twice.

brief: The user types in three whole numbers, one on each line.
The total is a whole number; the average is rounded to 1 decimal place.
questions.starter: # Three whole numbers in. Total, then the rounded average.

tests.why: 17.0 on the first line means / crept into the total. Adding whole numbers leaves a whole number.
This average is exact, and / still gives a real number, so the second line is 8.0 and not 8.
Divide the stored total, not just the last number: round(total / 3, 1).

questions.fb: Storing a value you need twice saves working it out twice, and it means both answers are certain to agree.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many items are bought and then the price of one item in pence. Work out the total cost in pence. Display [total pence], then [whole pounds in the total], then [pence left over], one on each line.

teach.say: Work the total out once and store it, then use // and % on that variable instead of working it out again.

brief: The user types in two lines: how many items, then the price of one in pence.
There are 100 pence in a pound.
Three lines of output: the total, the pounds, then the pence.
questions.starter: # How many and the price in. Total, pounds, pence.

tests.why: A long row of repeated digits on the first line means a string was multiplied. Cast both inputs with int().
There are 100 pence in a pound, so // 100 gives the 3 pounds and % 100 gives the 96 pence.
Exactly one pound leaves 0 pence over, and that 0 still has to be printed.

questions.fb: Real programs chain these together: cast the inputs, work out one total, then use // and % to show it in the form asked for.
